summaries.headline: Denver Board Considers Mandating Science of Reading Districtwide
summaries.summary: Denver school board members are weighing a policy that would require all schools to use science of reading-backed literacy instruction, citing stark disparities in implementation between affluent and lower-income schools. The proposed policy would also mandate early dyslexia identification and provide digital literacy apps for home practice, as board members point to achievement gaps where 67% of white third graders met state literacy expectations compared to just 26% of Black and 25% of Latino students. The move would formalize district-wide what Colorado already requires by state law, potentially closing gaps in how consistently schools apply research-backed reading methods.

summaries.headline: Reading Scores Decline Nationally Despite Math Recovery
summaries.summary: Students across the U.S. remain nearly half a grade level behind pre-pandemic reading scores, with researchers documenting a "reading recession" that began years before COVID-19 disrupted schools. Harvard, Stanford and Dartmouth scholars analyzed test data from over 5,000 districts in 38 states and found only five states plus D.C. showed meaningful reading growth from 2022 to 2025, while almost every state saw math improvements during the same period. The divergent trajectories suggest schools may need fundamentally different strategies to address reading challenges than the approaches that are helping students recover in mathematics.

summaries.headline: Time Allocation in Literacy Blocks Drives Uneven Outcomes
summaries.summary: A mid-Atlantic district invested heavily in structured literacy—expanding universal preschool, implementing daily two-hour literacy blocks, and providing common planning time—yet continued seeing wide disparities in K-2 reading scores between classrooms. SERP Institute observations revealed that how teachers allocate time within literacy blocks matters more than the blocks themselves, with students performing better when teachers routinely taught new vocabulary and encouraged multi-word responses during comprehension lessons rather than focusing solely on phonics. The findings suggest that districts implementing science of reading reforms may need to look beyond curriculum adoption to examine the granular decisions teachers make about instructional time and classroom discourse.

summaries.headline: Music Programs Target Early Literacy Through Singing
summaries.summary: Research shows singing helps young children learn vocabulary and develop phonological awareness, the ability to identify sounds in words that underlies reading skills. Nonprofits in Minnesota, Houston, and New York City are bringing free music programs into health clinics, early childhood centers, and other community spaces to reach families who lack access to costly children's music classes. The push comes as reading scores have stalled post-pandemic and experts worry that academic pressure is squeezing music and arts out of early childhood classrooms despite evidence of their developmental benefits.

summaries.headline: Chicago Principals Face Budget Cuts Despite Special Education Boost
summaries.summary: Chicago Public Schools sent principals their 2026-27 budgets Tuesday, marking the district's toughest financial season since before the pandemic as it confronts a deficit now exceeding $730 million. The budgets increase student-teacher ratios by one student per class and eliminate assistant principal positions at schools with fewer than 250 students—affecting about 120 positions—while boosting special education staffing and capping educator layoffs at four per elementary school and six per high school. The spending cuts, estimated at $96 million in school-level savings, reflect the end of nearly $3 billion in federal COVID relief that had funded almost 10,000 new positions since 2019 even as enrollment dropped by 45,000 students.

summaries.headline: Budget Pressures Force Districts to Cut DEI Positions
summaries.summary: School districts facing budget deficits are eliminating diversity, equity and inclusion offices despite community opposition, with at least four Massachusetts districts cutting DEI initiatives or positions this year. Brookline's school board voted 5-4 to close its equity office after pulling its $188,000 operations funding, rejecting more than $188,000 in community donations and denying a $25,000 state grant to recruit teachers of color. The cuts come as districts cite declining enrollment and reduced federal funding, while the Trump administration's stance on DEI creates additional pressure to scale back programs that supporters argue are essential for addressing racial disparities in schools.

summaries.headline: Colorado Lawmakers Target Homeschool Enrichment Funding Loopholes
summaries.summary: Colorado lawmakers passed amendments to restrict Boards of Cooperative Educational Services from authorizing public schools and homeschool enrichment programs outside their member districts, targeting a Monument-based co-op that has exploited state funding loopholes. Education reEnvisioned BOCES operates more than 50 enrichment programs created in recent years and opened what its leader called the state's "first public Christian school," costing the state tens of millions of dollars during budget constraints. The legislation represents months of legislative frustration over organizations using cooperative structures to access state funding for programs that stretch traditional public education boundaries.

summaries.headline: Chicago Board Debates Resolution on State School Funding
summaries.summary: Chicago school board members debated a resolution calling on state lawmakers to find new progressive revenue sources for schools, as the district released leaner campus budgets that prompted criticism from labor leaders. Several board members held a press conference arguing against a proposed Bears stadium project they claim would divert resources from schools, while union leaders criticized cuts to assistant principals and other positions as "disappointing" and "self-defeating." The debate highlights the tension between local advocacy efforts and Springfield lawmakers' signals that the state faces its own budget pressures, leaving districts to navigate funding shortfalls with limited options for relief.

summaries.headline: Denver Superintendent Signals More School Closures Coming
summaries.summary: Denver Superintendent Alex Marrero told the school board that more school closures will likely be necessary before the district's four-year closure moratorium expires, despite shuttering 10 schools last year due to declining enrollment. The district faces a projected $28 million cumulative deficit over five years as enrollment continues dropping from lower birth rates and high housing costs that push families out of the city. Marrero said he has "good confidence" closures could happen within two years, as fewer students mean less per-pupil state funding and tougher budget decisions ahead.

summaries.headline: Chicago Cut 500 Custodian Jobs, Schools Got Dirtier
summaries.summary: Chicago Public Schools eliminated nearly 500 custodian positions last summer to address budget shortfalls, cutting close to one-fifth of cleaning staff districtwide. A November survey of 168 principals and 423 custodians revealed three-quarters of principals lack adequate cleaning staff, with many reporting they now handle trash pickup and spill cleanup themselves while some schools face new pest problems. The custodial cuts highlight how districts managing massive deficits—Chicago faces a $700 million shortfall this year—must balance basic facility maintenance against other priorities, particularly as research links school cleanliness to student health and attendance rates.

summaries.headline: Colorado Passes AI Rules, School Funding Bills
summaries.summary: Colorado lawmakers advanced legislation regulating artificial intelligence use in psychotherapy and chatbot interactions with minors as the legislative session nears its Wednesday close. The House gave final approval to multiple bills including AI oversight measures and a financial mechanism allowing the state to redirect over-collected taxes beyond constitutional revenue limits. The Senate also moved forward a bill designed to preempt a November ballot initiative that would require over $500 million annually in dedicated road funding, potentially forcing difficult budget trade-offs that could affect education and other state priorities.

summaries.headline: Colorado Passes AI Regulations, School Funding Bills
summaries.summary: Colorado lawmakers advanced legislation regulating artificial intelligence use in schools and psychotherapy while finalizing tax measures to fund education and other state priorities as the legislative session nears its Wednesday conclusion. The House gave final approval to bills governing chat-bot interactions with minors and AI use in therapeutic settings, while the Senate moved forward a tax bill that eliminates exemptions on overtime wages and limits other deductions to generate revenue for renewable energy and wildfire mitigation programs. The flurry of final-day activity reflects the legislature's attempt to address emerging technology concerns while securing funding streams that could affect district budgets and student services statewide.

summaries.headline: Success Academy Alumni Question Academic Pressure's Price
summaries.summary: Former students of New York City's largest charter network are speaking out about their experiences as Success Academy marks its 20th anniversary. The network's test scores run nearly double those of traditional public school peers and boasts 100% college acceptance rates, but alumni describe lasting emotional effects from strict behavioral standards and intense academic pressure. Student voices now challenge whether high-performing schools can maintain their results without psychological costs that follow graduates beyond graduation.

summaries.headline: Ohio District Reverses English Learners' Pandemic Reading Losses
summaries.summary: Troy Public Schools in Ohio has rebuilt English learner literacy rates after the pandemic disrupted language acquisition for students still developing basic English skills. The district implemented a multi-sensory phonics approach combining visual cues, sounds, and movement, while expanding professional development for teachers working with English learners across all grade levels. The recovery demonstrates how targeted instructional shifts and teacher training can accelerate literacy gains for students whose language learning was most vulnerable to remote learning disruptions.

summaries.headline: School Districts Open Parking Lots for Homeless Families
summaries.summary: San Diego school district officials partnered with the city and nonprofits to convert district parking lots into temporary shelters for homeless students and their families, providing RV trailers with basic amenities while families work with caseworkers to find permanent housing. The initiative emerged as family homelessness hit record highs in 2024, with rising inflation and housing costs pushing more families with school-age children into unstable living situations. The model is spreading beyond California to other states as districts grapple with how to address the basic needs of students who can't focus on learning without stable housing.

summaries.headline: Canvas Owner Likely Paid Ransomware Demand After Breach
summaries.summary: Instructure, the company behind the Canvas learning management system used by millions of students, reached an "agreement" with cybercriminals following a data breach that exposed sensitive information. Cybersecurity experts interpret the company's carefully worded statement as evidence of a ransomware payment, a practice the FBI strongly discourages as it fuels further attacks. The incident highlights the vulnerability of educational technology platforms that store vast amounts of student and educator data, potentially setting a concerning precedent for how ed-tech companies respond to cyber threats.

summaries.headline: Colorado Districts Launch Online Programs to Reclaim Lost Students
summaries.summary: Colorado school districts are creating their own online programs to compete with multi-district virtual schools that have drawn students and state funding away from local communities. Delta County lost 138 students and $1.6 million in state dollars to online schools last year, prompting the district to launch its own virtual program that keeps students connected to local staff and activities. More than 30,000 Colorado students now attend multi-district online schools, with about half of those programs enrolling 90% or more of their students from outside their authorizing districts, creating a statewide competition for enrollment and per-pupil funding.

summaries.headline: NASA and Code.org Launch AI Education Resource
summaries.summary: NASA and Code.org released a new AI education resource featuring real-world space applications as 50 college teams prepare for the 2026 Lunabotics Challenge at Kennedy Space Center. The video connects AI concepts to current NASA work including Mars rover navigation, satellite imagery analysis, and exoplanet research, with NASA's AI lead emphasizing that the technology augments rather than replaces human decision-making. The timing aligns with growing demand for authentic STEM contexts that move beyond theoretical AI discussions to showcase how the technology operates in high-stakes, mission-critical environments.

summaries.headline: UNC System Develops Math Teaching Framework After Reading Success
summaries.summary: The UNC System has assembled 11 "math fellows" to create an evidence-based framework for elementary math instruction in teacher-preparation programs, following the successful but lengthy adoption of science of reading standards that took six years and required state legislation. System officials gathered education faculty from across North Carolina's public universities last month to share the new math teaching standards, hoping to avoid the protracted timeline that characterized the literacy overhaul completed just two years ago. The initiative reflects growing pressure to apply the same research-driven approach that transformed reading instruction to mathematics, where teacher training programs have similarly lacked consistency in their methods.

summaries.headline: Omaha Schools Implements Daily Structured Literacy Blocks
summaries.summary: Omaha Public Schools has instituted daily 75-minute structured literacy blocks across all elementary classrooms as part of Superintendent Matthew Ray's goal to have all students reading on grade level by 2030. Teachers report that the protected instructional time, which cannot be interrupted, has boosted student confidence not only in reading but across other subjects as students apply vocabulary and skills learned during the literacy block. The district's two-year implementation suggests that sustained, uninterrupted literacy instruction may be key to addressing reading proficiency gaps that many urban districts continue to face.

synthesis.topic_title: School Funding Gains Momentum as States Address Formula Reforms
synthesis.whats_happening: State lawmakers are advancing significant education funding increases while grappling with calls for deeper structural reforms to allocation formulas. Alaska legislators passed more than $140 million in additional education funding, Wisconsin approved what officials describe as historic funding boosts, and Maine faces growing pressure to overhaul its funding distribution system.
synthesis.whats_driving: Post-pandemic recovery needs continue driving legislative action on education budgets, while longstanding equity concerns about funding formulas gain political traction. Local communities remain engaged in budget approval processes even as state-level investments increase, suggesting ongoing gaps between available resources and community expectations.

local_articles.title: Wisconsin lawmakers approve historic school funding boost, but is it enough?
local_articles.summary: Wisconsin lawmakers approve historic school funding boost, but is it enough?  Racine County Eye
local_articles.full_content:
#### Keep up with stories that shape our region

Sign up

[Skip to content](https://racinecountyeye.com/2026/05/11/wisconsin-lawmakers-school-funding/#main)

![DHS Back to School childrens health, school funding, Wisconsin special education reimbursement](https://i0.wp.com/racinecountyeye.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/classroom-2093743_1280.jpg?fit=1280%2C914&quality=89&ssl=1)

A bipartisan deal struck by Gov. Tony Evers, Assembly Speaker Robin Vos (R-Rochester), and Senate Majority Leader Devin LeMahieu (R-Oostburg) would pour more than $600 million into Wisconsin’s K-12 schools, push the state’s special education reimbursement rate to 50%, and deliver property tax relief to homeowners statewide.

The package was announced Monday in a press release from Evers’ office.

The deal also eliminates state income taxes on tips and overtime pay, and returns more than $850 million in surplus funds directly to Wisconsin taxpayers. The Wisconsin Legislature’s Joint Committee on Finance is set to take up the proposal May 12, with full floor votes in both chambers expected May 13. Gov. Evers anticipates signing the legislation as early as next week.

[Racine Unified School District](http://rusd.org/)(RUSD) Superintendent Soren Gajewski put the local stakes plainly when speaking at a [Gateway Technical College town hall in June 2025](https://racinecountyeye.com/2025/06/25/special-education-funding-state-wi/).

“We have $38.2 million that are diverted to special education funding out of our regular budget,” he said. “That’s money that would otherwise go into reading programs, STEM, arts — all of that.”

## **Special education funding**

The release touts an additional $300 million for special education aid, which the state says will bring the reimbursement rate to 50% in 2026-27, effectively doubling what it was when Evers took office in 2019.

That number matters in part because the last budget promise on special education fell apart almost immediately.

When the 2025-27 state budget was signed in July, lawmakers said it would reimburse districts at 42% in the first year and 45% in the second. By [November 2025, the state Department of Public Instruction](https://racinecountyeye.com/2025/11/21/special-education-reimbursement-35/) (DPI) notified districts that initial payments would cover only 35% of costs, well below what had been promised.

The reason: the special education appropriation was structured as “sum certain” — a fixed dollar amount — rather than “sum sufficient,” meaning a guaranteed percentage. When actual costs exceeded projections, the reimbursement rate fell short. The new deal appears to address that structural flaw, though the final bill language should be confirmed before publication.

Rep. Angelina Cruz (D-Racine) introduced legislation in November 2025 to close that gap using the state’s surplus.

“This is the easiest fix we can make with a budget that’s already been set,” Cruz said at the time. “It’s a chance for legislators to make good on their promise to support public schools — no excuses.”

The bipartisan deal announced Monday goes further than Cruz’s bill proposed.

Even at 50%, the state would still leave half of every dollar districts spend on special education unreimbursed. Private and charter schools participating in the state’s voucher programs already receive a 90% reimbursement rate.

Advocates have long called for public schools to receive at least 60%, and ideally 90%, reimbursement, a level the state has never reached for public schools.

Cruz has not provided a statement about the deal. Racine County Eye will update this article when she does.

## **$300 million in general school aids**

Beyond special education, the deal includes $300 million in general school aids, the largest form of state support for Wisconsin’s 421 public school districts.

That money flows through an equalization formula designed to account for differences in local property wealth. Districts with lower property values per pupil, like Racine Unified, generally receive a larger share of state aid than wealthier districts.

The $300 million represents roughly a 5% increase in the general school aid pool, which totaled about $5.58 billion in 2024-25. How much any individual district benefits depends on its enrollment, spending levels, and local property values; there is no flat per-district or per-pupil check.

DPI will calculate district-level amounts once the legislation is signed.

The infusion matters because more state aid directly reduces how much districts need to collect from local property taxes. Wisconsin school property taxes rose 7.8% in December 2025, the largest increase in more than three decades, as a result in large part by flat state support, according to a Wisconsin Policy Forum report. That forced many districts to make up the difference through local levies.

## **The structural problem this deal doesn’t fix**

To understand why school funding has become a perennial crisis, it helps to understand what happened in 2009.

Wisconsin school districts had their per-pupil revenue limits, the cap on combined state aid and local property tax revenue, automatically adjusted each year to keep pace with inflation. When the Great Recession hit, a Democratic-controlled Legislature and Gov. Jim Doyle removed that automatic adjustment to protect property taxpayers during a period of economic upheaval.

It was widely understood to be a temporary measure, but it was never restored.

According to the [Wisconsin Association of School Business Official](http://according%20to%20the%20wisconsin%20association%20of%20school%20business%20officials,%20school%20funding%20today%20lags%20inflation%20by%20roughly%20$3,400%20per%20pupil%20per%20year%20compared%20to%202009%20levels/) s and advocacy groups such as the [Wisconsin Network for Public Education](https://www.wisconsinnetwork.org/funding), school funding today lags inflation by roughly $3,400 per pupil per year compared to 2009 levels.

Closing that gap entirely would require billions in new spending, not the $300 million this deal provides.

## **Property tax relief**

The deal provides $350 million in total property tax relief: the $300 million in general school aids described above, plus an additional $50 million directed to the Wisconsin Technical College System, which includes Gateway Technical College.

Under state law, that technical college aid is counted against each district’s revenue limit, reducing the local levy by an equal amount, meaning it functions as a direct property tax cut rather than a general fund transfer.

Racine County property taxpayers already absorbed some of the steepest increases in the state last December — part of a statewide 7.8% spike in school levies, the largest increase in more than three decades, according to a [Wisconsin Policy Forum report](https://racinecountyeye.com/2025/12/22/wisconsin-property-tax-increase/) included in a story from Wisconsin Examiner.

More state aid flowing to districts directly reduces what they need to collect locally, but how much any individual property tax bill drops won’t be known until DPI certifies aid amounts after the legislation is signed.

## **No tax on tips and overtime**

For Racine County workers in occupations such as restaurant servers, bartenders, salon workers, hotel staff, and others, the deal would eliminate Wisconsin state income taxes on tip income, mirroring a federal provision enacted last July as part of the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Under federal law, workers in eligible tipped occupations can deduct up to $25,000 in qualifying tips from their taxable income. The deduction covers voluntary tips received in cash, by credit card or through a tip pool, and is available whether a worker itemizes deductions or takes the standard deduction. The federal provision applies to tax years 2025 through 2028 and then expires. The Wisconsin version would be permanent.

A server earning $20,000 in tips who falls in the 22% federal tax bracket saves $4,400 in federal income taxes under the federal provision. At Wisconsin’s applicable state income tax rate, the state-level savings would add several hundred to over a thousand dollars on top of that, depending on total income.

Workers should note that Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes (FICA) still apply to tips under both federal and state law. The exemption covers income tax only.

For overtime, only the premium portion, the extra half of time-and-a-half pay, is deductible, not the full overtime paycheck. The federal deduction caps at $12,500 for single filers and $25,000 for joint filers, with the same income phase-outs as the tips provision. The state projects eliminating income tax on overtime will save Wisconsin families $328 million over the next two years.

## **What comes next**

The Joint Committee on Finance takes up the proposal Tuesday, May 12, and full Assembly and Senate floor votes are expected Wednesday, May 13.

If signed as early as next week, some school funding could reach districts before the current fiscal year ends June 30.

Gajewski said Racine Unified is still assessing what the package means locally.

“We appreciate our legislators working together to provide any additional support for our public schools – specifically, much-needed funding for special education,” he said in a statement sent to media. “Over the coming days, we’ll work to determine the full impact on our district budget.”

# Alaska House passes bill adding more than $140 million to education budget

By [Iris Samuels](https://www.adn.com/author/iris-samuels)

Published: May 12, 2026

![](https://www.adn.com/resizer/v2/EFGQJLXCMRBYTCAWYKYCKUAYJ4.JPG?auth=a6497e92dabd1969f02d5f5817701926a2cb1309c6e1a749d2406e6b6ff3f6b0&width=800&height=533)Rep. Andi Story, D-Juneau, speaks on the House floor at the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau on May 19, 2025. (Marc Lester / ADN)

JUNEAU — The Alaska House voted Tuesday to alter the method for calculating education funding and boost state expenditures on public schools by over $140 million annually.

But the bill, which passed the House in a 31-9 vote with bipartisan support, is unlikely to pass in the Senate in its current form before the expected end of the session later this month, according to key lawmakers.

The legislation comes on top of promises from both the House and Senate to include one-time funding of up to [$158 million](https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/2026/03/24/alaska-house-majority-seeks-to-guarantee-158m-increase-in-public-school-funding/ "https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/2026/03/24/alaska-house-majority-seeks-to-guarantee-158m-increase-in-public-school-funding/") for K-12 schools in the coming fiscal year, on top of a base budget of roughly $1.4 billion for Alaska’s roughly 130,000 schoolchildren.

Still, provisions from the House bill, which was sponsored by Juneau Democratic Rep. Andi Story, could be added to an [education omnibus bill](https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/2026/04/22/alaska-senate-committee-fast-tracks-one-time-education-funding-measures/) that is set to be heard in the Senate before the end of the session.

“There are definitely components that I think will make it into the final negotiations on the end package. What they look like is still to be seen,” Sen. Löki Tobin, chair of the Senate Education Committee, said Tuesday.

The House-passed bill would substantially increase state funding for schools by basing their funding on previous years’ enrollment, rather than current attendance. The change would be significant in part because the state has seen declining public school enrollment, driving down total education spending despite lawmakers [intentions to increase](https://www.adn.com/politics/alaska-legislature/2025/05/20/alaska-lawmakers-override-dunleavys-veto-of-education-bill/) it.

“Part of what I feel is so hurting parents’ confidence in our system is our broken timeline process,” Story said during a floor debate on the bill.

ADVERTISEMENT

“School communities routinely do not learn their final funding levels for the upcoming school year until late May, after critical staffing and program decisions must be made,” she said.

The state education department [estimated](https://www.akleg.gov/PDF/34/F/HB0261-5-3-050626-EED-Y.PDF) that the altered student count process would increase state spending on schools by $113 million annually, including $31 million for the Anchorage School District, $13 million for the Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District, $12 million for the Fairbanks North Star Borough district, and nearly $12 million for Juneau schools.

In a last-minute change, lawmakers also voted 24-16 on Monday to add a provision to the bill that would shift tens of millions in education costs from cities and boroughs to the state.

That change, which was introduced as an amendment by Soldotna Republican Rep. Justin Ruffridge and drew support from both minority and majority members, is meant to reverse what has been a gradual transfer of K-12 school costs from state coffers to local taxpayers.

ADVERTISEMENT

Under the existing funding formula, the amount that boroughs and cities are expected to contribute to school districts is a function of local property value. As growth in property value has outpaced increases to the state’s school funding formula, boroughs and cities have faced pressure to raise local taxation to keep up with education costs.

Under Ruffridge’s amendment, the annual growth in the local contribution rates would be capped at 2%, essentially untethering the contribution rates from property values.

That change is [expected](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/get_documents.asp?session=34&docid=12426) to shift nearly $30 million in school costs from local cities and boroughs to the state in the first year after the bill’s passage. Based on projected increases in property values, the measure would shift tens of millions in additional dollars each subsequent year.

The change is supported by leaders of several of the largest communities in the state, including Anchorage Mayor Suzanne LaFrance, who wrote in a [letter](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/get_documents.asp?session=34&docid=15569) to lawmakers last month that the expectation that local taxpayers shoulder a growing burden of school costs “has strained municipalities and undermined the stable partnership our education system depends on.”

“By modernizing the required local contribution formula and limiting annual increases to no more than two percent, this bill creates a more predictable and sustainable framework for both local governments and school districts,” LaFrance wrote, speaking about a version of the legislation that was introduced earlier this year in the Senate.

ADVERTISEMENT

But Tobin, an Anchorage Democrat, said the proposed change over time could create inequities among school districts. Disconnecting the local contribution expectation from property values could mean that eventually, fast-growing communities contribute a smaller share from their local tax base when compared with regions of the state that have a stable or shrinking population.

The current situation, Tobin said, was not anticipated by the authors of the school funding formula: a decade of stagnant state funding for schools, local property values that skyrocketed after the pandemic, and declining school enrollment.

“It is a perfect storm, and I fully appreciate the shifting of the burden onto our local municipalities to continue to fund their schools,” said Tobin.

However, she said “there needs to be significant consideration given to an equitable way that we fund all school districts.”

The House bill “doesn’t quite meet the mark,” she said.

Tobin said she is still focused on a wide-ranging education bill that was introduced last month. That measure, which is currently under consideration in the Senate Finance Committee, would implement a new loan repayment program for a limited number of teachers, provide grants for reading improvement, increase funding for career and technical education, and provide more money for student transportation.

A new version of the legislation is expected before the end of the session, Tobin said, potentially incorporating pieces of Story’s bill.

“There are concepts that are in that legislation that I think are really needed to help stabilize our education funding and bring some predictability to our districts. Unfortunately, I think there’s some holes that need to be filled,” said Tobin. “Do I think we have the bandwidth and the capacity to close those and then get it across the finish line? That’s going to be a heavy lift.”

The education funding debate on the House floor brought to the fore concerns about other factors increasing the cost of educating Alaska’s children, including health insurance and heating fuel.

An effort sponsored by Homer Republican Rep. Sarah Vance to amend the bill to allow school districts to join a state-sponsored health insurance pool, rather than negotiating their plans individually, failed narrowly in a 21-19 vote.

“Why aren’t we asking how we can save money — energy costs, health care costs — the huge ones that are sucking the air out of the room of the school districts’ funding?"Vance said. “We’re so far behind what we could be offering as far as education, and we keep trying to pick up the pieces, and we can’t move quick enough because we’re not listening.”

House members who supported the bill said it was a needed follow-up to last year’s hard-won permanent increase to the education funding factor known as the Base Student Allocation. Legislators for several years had attempted to overcome Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s [opposition](https://www.adn.com/politics/2025/05/19/gov-dunleavy-vetoes-bipartisan-education-funding-bill-as-lawmakers-say-override-possible/ "https://www.adn.com/politics/2025/05/19/gov-dunleavy-vetoes-bipartisan-education-funding-bill-as-lawmakers-say-override-possible/") to stand-alone education funding bills. They finally succeeded last year, twice overriding Dunleavy’s vetoes to do so.

Even after lawmakers raised the BSA by $700 — from $5,960 to $6,660 — the state’s spending on schools declined this year compared to the previous year’s spending. The final figure is calculated based on a complicated formula that is predicated on the number of students enrolled in Alaska schools, among other factors.

“Under current law, if property tax assessments rise faster than the BSA, then, perversely, that cuts state funding for schools. That makes no sense,” said Anchorage Democratic Rep. Zack Fields. “Is fixing the local contribution problem sufficient on its own? No, it’s not. We also have to keep pace with funding with the BSA, but I just don’t understand why we would leave in place an antiquated statute.”

**Rep. Kelly Murphy** _, D-Scarborough, represents District 125, which includes part of Scarborough. She is the House chair of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee._

For far too long, Maine’s Essential Programs and Services (EPS) school funding formula, which determines how much money each public school district receives from the state, hasn’t been working well for the vast majority of our communities.

This session, the Legislature finally made important progress to fix some of the formula’s chronic problems — changes that will benefit Maine students, educators and property taxpayers across the state.

The EPS formula was passed by the Legislature in 2000 and first implemented in 2005. Its goal was to provide the state with a mechanism for establishing a minimum sufficient funding level to ensure all pre-K to 12th grade-level students could meet the [Maine Learning Results](https://www.maine.gov/doe/learning/diplomas/MaineLearningResults) standards. It also aimed to create a fair, equitable funding split between local communities and the state.

Prior to this session, EPS hadn’t been significantly altered in over 20 years, but a lot has changed over that time. Most notably, property valuations in many communities have skyrocketed — especially since 2020 — creating a big disparity between property valuations and residents’ actual ability to pay.

This has made EPS less effective and more inequitable over time, leaving a lot of communities to pay for more than their reasonable share of public education. Maine now has one of the highest levels of reliance on property tax in the nation for school funding.

Advertisement

Other major changes over the last two decades include declining student enrollment, increasing student needs and educator workforce shortages. The formula has also done a poor job of taking into account special education costs and students from economically disadvantaged households.

Recognizing this, in 2024, the Legislature’s Education and Cultural Affairs Committee asked the Maine Education Policy Research Institute to study the impacts of how the formula distributes state funds among districts across the state. They reported back to the committee last year with their assessment, along with some potential changes that could result in a better EPS formula.

Some of these recommendations were included in [LD 2226](https://legislature.maine.gov/LawMakerWeb/summary.asp?ID=280101812), a bill developed by the Department of Education and which I presented to the committee in my capacity as chair. Ultimately, the bill passed the Legislature with overwhelming bipartisan support — [122-23](https://legislature.maine.gov/LawMakerWeb/rollcall.asp?ID=280101812&chamber=House&serialnumber=806) in the House and [28-6](https://legislature.maine.gov/LawMakerWeb/rollcall.asp?ID=280101812&chamber=Senate&serialnumber=947) in the Senate — before it was signed by Gov. Janet Mills.

As amended, the bill focuses on fixing two of the formula’s provisions: updating regional cost adjustments and modifying the ability‑to‑contribute calculation. Existing regional adjustment factors are outdated, based on historic salary data and misaligned with the current minimum teacher salary framework. Changing the ability-to-contribute framework will also help ease the burden on communities with rapidly rising property values and flat or fixed household incomes.

With these changes, most communities will experience an increase in funding support from the state. Only 11 districts — including Scarborough, which I represent — will see reductions. To help mitigate the loss of funding, I deliberately worked with stakeholders to delay the phasing in of these changes until 2030, which will lessen the immediate impacts on school budgets and give districts time to adapt while further adjustments are made to the formula. It’s not a perfect solution, but it will do the least amount of harm for districts that will be negatively affected.

These changes to the EPS formula represent only a handful of policies we passed this year that will support K-12 public education throughout Maine. We also passed bills to provide $8 million in one-time bridge funding for 193 school districts, provide $2 million for the Building Assets, Reducing Risks program to backfill lost federal funds, close gaps in our universal school meals program and phase in an increase in minimum teacher salaries from $40,000 to $50,000.

Together, these measures will go a long way to strengthen K-12 public education in Maine, but the EPS formula changes are some of the most consequential. It’s a critical start to fixing a broken formula that is long overdue — and it will have lasting, positive impacts on our entire state in the years to come.

# Hawley residents pass education budget

Nineteen Hawley residents voted in favor of the education budget, $676,165 for the upcoming fiscal year with the most significant increase being the vocational school budget which more than doubled from $70,000 to $190,000.

By Franklin County Now May 14, 2026 8:03 am

![](https://franklincountynow.com/wp-content/themes/franklincountynow/screenshot.png)

HAWLEY, MA ( [FRANKLIN COUNTY NOW](https://franklincountynow.com/)) — Nineteen Hawley residents voted in favor of the education budget, $676,165 for the upcoming fiscal year with the most significant increase being the vocational school budget which more than doubled from $70,000 to $190,000.

The article with the most discussion was centered around paying extra expenses from snow removal this past winter and whether the funds should come from the stabilization account or the revolving fund. Ultimately, it was voted to use funds from the Highway Stabilization Account to pay the deficit.

# Franklin Tech knocks off Turners Falls softball on Senior Night

By Jeff Tirrell May 13, 2026 2:20 pm

- [Facebook](https://franklincountynow.com/news/216612-franklin-tech-knocks-off-turners-falls-softball-on-senior-night/?share=facebook)

![Female softball pitcher in a gray Franklin uniform releasing a neon yellow ball on a dirt mound at night, wearing a protective mask and cleats.](https://franklincountynow.com/wp-content/blogs.dir/261/files/2026/05/FC-Tech-softball-1-1200x768.jpg)Franklin County NowChip Cormie

![](https://franklincountynow.com/wp-content/themes/franklincountynow/screenshot.png)

TURNERS FALLS, MA ( [FRANKLIN COUNTY NOW](http://franklincountynow.com/)) — The Franklin Tech softball team took an early lead and later rallied from a deficit to beat the Turners Falls Thunder on their Senior Night, 10-6 in Franklin County League play on Tuesday night.

The Eagles took a quick 3-0 lead in the top of the first inning, highlighted by a two-run single by Charly Knight, only to see the Thunder tie it at 3 in the bottom half of the inning. Abby Moffatt’s two-out, two-run single tied the score at 3.

After Franklin Tech went back up 4-3 in the second inning on a leadoff home run by Lindsey Taylor, Turners Falls once again drew even at 4-4 in the bottom of the frame.

The Thunder scored two runs in the third to take a 6-4 lead, but Franklin Tech starting pitcher Brayleigh Burgh shut them down the rest of the way.

The Eagles took control of the contest with a four-run outburst in the fifth, keyed by a bases-clearing three-run triple by Taylor, who had three hits, four runs batted in, and three runs scored on the night.

Franklin Tech upped its record to 5-11, while Turners Falls fell to 6-10.

The pregame Senior Night festivities honored Turners Falls seniors Maddie Dietz and Janelle Massey. The senior players from Franklin Tech were also acknowledged by the Turners Falls team.
